class.name: TerrainGenerator3D
class.brief_description: Generates mountain ranges for a whole world by tectonic uplift against fluvial erosion, and writes them into the ground.
class.description: Simulates the large-scale landscape model of Cordonnier et al. 2016 ("Large Scale Terrain Generation from Tectonic Uplift and Fluvial Erosion"): rock rises at an uplift rate [code]U[/code], and rivers cut it by the stream power law [code]dh/dt = U - K A^m S[/code] (drainage area [code]A[/code], slope [code]S[/code]). Run towards equilibrium, the two make mountain ranges with connected, branching river valleys and the ridges between them, where uplift is high. The implicit solver of Braun and Willett 2013 makes every step stable at any [member time_step]. Closed basins are filled with sediment (Priority-Flood, Barnes et al. 2014), slopes are held under [member critical_slope], [member hillslope_diffusion] rounds hilltops, and drainage area is routed to all lower neighbours ([member flow_exponent]) so valleys do not follow the grid. Where the rock rises is the input: [member base_uplift] everywhere, a painted [member uplift_map] over the rectangle, Path3D [member ranges] (a band of [member range_width] around each curve), and an [member uplift_noise] that breaks them up. The grid is [member size] metres centred on the node, every [member cell_size] metres; a coarse cell size (8 to 32 m) is intended, since this is the world's large-scale shape. [method bake] (the inspector's Generate button) runs [method generate] then [method write_to_terrain], which samples the result bicubically onto the ground: a [code]Terrain3D[/code] node (called by name, never required; missing regions are created) or a [CollisionShape3D] with a [HeightMapShape3D], with an optional [member ground_mesh]. With a [member deformer], its brushes (rivers, roads, plots) are lifted before the write and applied again on the new ground. The simulation is single-threaded and runs in a fixed order, so the same settings and [member seed] give the same terrain on every machine. Only the starting roughness depends on the seed; it decides which drainage network forms. The result is not saved with the node (the ground keeps it). [method get_height], [method get_drainage_area] and [method get_sediment_depth] read it after [method generate].

method.name: bake
method.description: [method generate] then [method write_to_terrain]. Returns the number of vertices written.

method.name: build_river_paths
method.description: Adds one path per river from [method get_rivers] under [param parent]: a [code]PhysXRiver3D[/code] when that class exists (curve, [code]widths[/code], its own discharge, and [code]mouth_target[/code] set to the river it joins, or to the sea or lake it ends in when [method build_water] made them), otherwise a [Path3D] with the widths, discharge and joined river as metadata. Points are converted into [param parent]'s space. In the editor the paths are owned by the edited scene. Returns the new nodes, trunk rivers first.

method.name: build_water
method.description: Creates the water of the last [method generate] under [param parent] and returns the nodes: a [code]PhysXWaterSurface3D[/code] (by class name, when the PhysX module is in the build) for the sea, at sea level over the generated rectangle with [code]seabed_from_floor[/code], [code]shore_waves[/code], [code]open_sea_beyond[/code] and [code]follow_weather[/code] on and three [code]wave_cascades[/code], and one per lake at its level with [code]surface_mesh[/code] set to the lake's outline and [code]follow_weather[/code] on. Without the PhysX module, plain [MeshInstance3D] sheets. Call it after the ground is written (the water reads its seabed through physics) and before [method build_river_paths], which then sets each river's [code]mouth_target[/code] to the sea or lake it ends in.

method.name: clear_result
method.description: Frees the generated grids.

method.name: generate
method.description: Runs [member steps] steps of uplift and erosion from a flat, slightly rough start. Returns [code]false[/code] if [member size] is empty.

method.name: get_base_height
method.description: The simulated ground at a world position, without the detail filter. NaN outside the rectangle or before [method generate].

method.name: get_detail_shader_code
get_discharge
method.description: Mean discharge in m³/s of a drainage area [param area] in m² at [member river_runoff].

method.name: get_discharge_at
method.description: Discharge in m³/s at the grid node nearest [param global_position] in [param month] (0 January to 11 December; -1 the annual mean). With a [member climate_recipe], each month's runoff accumulated down the rivers (lakes lose their evaporation); without, [method get_discharge] of its drainage area.

method.name: get_drainage_area
method.description: Upstream drainage area at a world position, in square metres. Large values are rivers. NaN outside the rectangle or before [method generate].

method.name: get_drainage_image
method.description: Drainage area per grid node, [constant Image.FORMAT_RF], square metres.

method.name: get_geology_at
method.description: Soil depth (m), rock exposure (0..1), talus (0..1) and log10 of the drainage area (m²) at a world position, as a [Color] (r, g, b, a).

method.name: get_geology_image
method.description: The geology map, one texel per grid node, as an [constant Image.FORMAT_RGBAF] image: soil depth (m), rock exposure, talus, log10 drainage area.

method.name: get_geology_shader_code
method.description: Shader code declaring the [code]terrain_geology_map[/code] and [code]terrain_geology_rect[/code] shader globals and a function [code]vec4 terrain_geology(vec3 world_pos)[/code] returning what [method get_geology_at] returns. Paste it into a spatial shader, for example a terrain material that blends rock, scree and grass.

method.name: get_geology_texture
method.description: The geology map as a texture, updated by [method generate]. Also published as the [code]terrain_geology_map[/code] shader global when [member publish_shader_globals] is on.

method.name: get_grid_size
method.description: Grid nodes along X and Z of the last [method generate].

method.name: get_height
method.description: Generated ground height at a world position: the simulation (bicubic between grid nodes, including [member height_offset]) plus the detail filter. This is exactly what [method write_to_terrain] writes at a vertex. NaN outside the rectangle or before [method generate].

method.name: get_height_image
method.description: Generated heights per grid node, [constant Image.FORMAT_RF], metres.

method.name: get_inflow_cells
method.description: Where land beyond the map drains in ([member inflows]): a [Dictionary] per node with [code]position[/code] (on the ground) and [code]area[/code] (m²).

method.name: get_lake_result_count
method.description: Number of lakes the last [method generate] made.

method.name: get_lake_results
method.description: The lakes of the last [method generate], one [Dictionary] each: [code]level[/code], [code]bed[/code] and [code]depth[/code] (m), [code]area[/code] and [code]catchment[/code] (m²), [code]endorheic[/code] (no outflow: evaporation takes all its water), [code]center[/code] (the point on the water farthest from its shore), [code]rect[/code] (world XZ), [code]dam[/code] (the dam's spillway, on the ground) and [code]outlet[/code] (where the water leaves; absent when it has none).

method.name: get_last_change
method.description: Largest height change in the last step, in metres. Small against [member uplift] times [member time_step] means the landscape is close to equilibrium.

method.name: get_last_coarse_levels
method.description: Coarser grids the last [method generate] ran on (0: one level).

method.name: get_last_deposition_passes
method.description: Deposition passes the last [method generate] ran, over all steps and levels (0 with [member deposition] 0). Each step solves the deposition exactly in two sweeps, then runs passes until no node moves 5 cm; one or two a step is usual.

method.name: get_last_generate_msec
method.description: Time the last [method generate] took, in milliseconds.

method.name: get_last_runoff_msec
method.description: Time the last [method generate] spent on the climate and the water balance, in milliseconds (0 without a [member climate_recipe]).

method.name: get_last_steps
method.description: Steps the last [method generate] ran, over all levels.

method.name: get_last_tile_erosion_msec
method.description: Time the last tile erosion took, in milliseconds (part of [method get_last_generate_msec]).

method.name: get_last_water_msec
method.description: Time the coast, the lakes and the rivers' routing through them took in the last [method generate], in milliseconds (part of [method get_last_generate_msec]).

method.name: get_last_write_msec
method.description: Time the last [method write_to_terrain] took, in milliseconds.

method.name: get_mean_runoff
method.description: Mean runoff over the land of the last [method generate] with a [member climate_recipe], in mm a year. Lakes balance their inflow and evaporation with it.

method.name: get_last_sky_msec
method.description: Milliseconds the last sky occlusion bake took (see [member sky_occlusion]).

method.name: get_last_sky_light_msec
method.description: Milliseconds the last [method update_sky_light] took.

method.name: get_river_sites
method.description: Places along the rivers of [method get_rivers] ([param min_area]) for lakes and falls: every river point carrying at least [param min_discharge] m³/s in [member river_month], with how far the river drops over the next [param run] metres. Each is a [Dictionary]: [code]position[/code] (on the ground), [code]discharge[/code], [code]area[/code] (drainage, m²), [code]drop[/code] (m over the run), [code]run[/code] (m actually measured, shorter near a mouth), [code]river[/code] and [code]index[/code] (as in [method get_rivers]). For a lake that feeds a visible fall, pick a point with enough discharge and a large drop below it, and put a lake marker (with [code]rock_lip[/code] metadata) there.

method.name: get_rivers
method.description: Rivers draining at least [param min_area] m², trunk rivers first. Channels follow the receivers of the erosion run (D8 area, so it grows downstream); each river runs upstream from an outlet or junction along the donor with the largest area (Hack's main stem), and the other donors start tributaries. Each river is a [Dictionary]: [code]points[/code] ([PackedVector3Array], world, head to mouth, on the ground, smoothed), [code]widths[/code] (m, from the discharge: [code]width = river_width_coefficient * discharge^0.5[/code], Leopold and Maddock 1953), [code]areas[/code], [code]discharge[/code] (m³/s at the mouth, in [member river_month]), [code]monthly_discharge[/code] ([PackedFloat32Array], the twelve months at the mouth), [code]own_discharge[/code] (that minus its tributaries'), [code]joins[/code] (index of the river it joins, -1 at an outlet), [code]ends_in[/code] ([code]"sea"[/code], [code]"lake"[/code], [code]"river"[/code] or [code]"edge"[/code]), [code]lake[/code] (the lake it ends in, else -1) and [code]from_lake[/code] (the lake whose outflow it is, else -1). A tributary's last point is the junction on the river it joins. Rivers end at the first cell of the sea or a lake, on the water; a lake's outflow starts at its outlet and carries its whole catchment.

method.name: get_rock_exposure
method.description: How bare the rock is at a world position, 0 (covered) to 1 (bare): where the loose cover (soil, basin fill, alluvium) is thinner than about 0.3 m, less any talus. 0 before [method generate].

method.name: get_rock_hardness
method.description: The rock at the surface with [member strata_enabled]: 1 in a hard band, 0 in soft rock, the contacts blended over about 2 m. 0 with the strata off or before [method generate].

method.name: get_runoff_at
method.description: Water leaving the ground at a position for the rivers, in mm: in [param month] (0 January to 11 December), or a year with -1. A monthly water balance (McCabe and Markstrom 2007) of the [member climate_recipe]'s climate: rain and snow split by temperature, the snowpack melting by degree days and sunshine (Hock 1999), a soil water store losing Thornthwaite evapotranspiration (Thornthwaite and Mather 1957), a share of the rain running off at once and the rest of the surplus through a groundwater store. Without a recipe, [member river_runoff].

method.name: get_sediment_depth
method.description: Thickness of sediment that filled closed basins during the simulation, in metres: flat valley floors and old lake beds.

method.name: get_sediment_image
method.description: Sediment thickness per grid node, [constant Image.FORMAT_RF], metres.

method.name: get_sky_image
method.description: One layer of the ground's seen sky, [member sky_cell] apart from the result's corner: RGBA half of the nine spherical harmonics (luminance, over the whole sky's first) of the sky each node sees past its horizons, harmonics 0 to 3 in [param layer] 0, 4 to 7 in 1, 8 in 2. Published to shaders as the [code]terrain_sky_map[/code] array, with [code]terrain_sky_rect[/code] and the whole sky's harmonics in [code]terrain_sky_full[/code], [code]terrain_sky_full2[/code] and [code]terrain_sky_full3[/code]. Empty without [member sky_occlusion].

method.name: get_sky_visibility
method.description: The sky view factor at [param global_position], 0 to 1 (1 without [member sky_occlusion]).

method.name: get_snow_water_at
method.description: Snow water equivalent (mm) lying at a position at the end of [param month] (0 January to 11 December), from the water balance of [method get_runoff_at]. 0 without a [member climate_recipe]. Cells that never melt out keep gaining (a glacier's accumulation; its flow is not modelled).

method.name: get_soil_depth
method.description: Depth of loose cover at a world position, in metres: soil from the exponential soil production function (Heimsath et al. 1997) where production [member soil_production] meets the local erosion rate (channel incision plus hillslope creep), stripped on slopes near [member critical_slope]; plus basin fill; plus alluvium on channels gentle for their drainage area (channel steepness index well below that of the fastest-uplifting ground, Wobus et al. 2006).

method.name: get_talus
method.description: Scree at a world position, 0..1: shed by bare rock steeper than [member talus_angle], carried down the receivers and laid where the slope eases below it, thinning over [member talus_reach]; none on channels.

method.name: get_tile_deposit
method.description: Sediment laid down at a world position by tile erosion, in metres (alluvial fans, valley fills, scree aprons). 0 when [member tile_erosion_enabled] is off.

method.name: get_tile_flow
method.description: Water that passed a world position during tile erosion (droplet water per droplet started, time-averaged): high in streams and gullies, for wetness and stream textures. 0 when [member tile_erosion_enabled] is off or before [method generate].

method.name: get_uplift_image
method.description: The uplift rate used per grid node, [constant Image.FORMAT_RF], millimetres per year.

method.name: get_water_depth
method.description: Depth of the sea or a lake over the ground at a point; 0 on dry ground.

method.name: get_water_image
method.description: Water depth over the grid (m, 0 on dry ground), FORMAT_RF.

method.name: get_water_level
method.description: Height of the water surface (the sea's or a lake's) over a point; NaN on dry ground or outside.

method.name: get_waterfalls
method.description: Waterfalls along the rivers of [method get_rivers] ([param min_area]): runs of the channel steeper than 45 degrees in the eroded ground that drop at least [param min_height] m. Soft rock never stands steeper than [member critical_slope], so they form where rivers cut the hard bands of [member strata_enabled]. Each is a [Dictionary]: [code]top[/code] and [code]bottom[/code] (the lip and the foot, on the ground), [code]height[/code], [code]width[/code] and [code]discharge[/code] (of the river at the lip), [code]river[/code] (index in [method get_rivers]), [code]index[/code] (the lip's point in that river) and [code]hardness[/code] (of the rock at the lip; a lip that has just broken off stands on soft rock for a while), [code]face_run[/code] (m the face recedes over the drop: 3 where [member fall_lips] keeps it vertical), [code]jet_throw[/code] (m a free jet from the brink travels out over the drop, at critical flow) and [code]free_fall[/code] (the jet clears the face: a plunge rather than a cascade).

method.name: get_world_rect
method.description: The world X and Z rectangle the generator covers ([code]position.y[/code] is Z).

method.name: has_result
method.description: Whether [method generate] has run since the node was created or [method clear_result].

method.name: has_runoff
method.description: Whether the last [method generate] had a [member climate_recipe], so rivers carry rain and snowmelt by month.

method.name: has_sea_result
method.description: Whether the last [method generate] made any sea.

method.name: sample_heights
method.description: The final ground (as [method get_height]) on a regular grid of [param size] points starting at world [param origin] (x, z), [param spacing] metres apart, as an [constant Image.FORMAT_RF] image. Rows are computed in parallel. Points outside the rectangle are NaN.

method.name: write_to_terrain
method.description: Writes the generated heights into the ground's vertices inside the rectangle. Returns the number written.

method.name: update_sky_light
method.description: Weighs each node's seen sky by the light of [param panorama], a radiance panorama as [method RenderingServer.sky_bake_panorama] returns it, and updates the sky texture. [member sky_light_source] does this by itself. Returns [code]false[/code] without a sky occlusion bake.

members.member: Exponent [code]m[/code] of drainage area in the stream power law (slope exponent [code]n = 1[/code]). 0.4 to 0.6 is typical of real rivers; higher concentrates erosion in big valleys.
Uplift strength everywhere, 0 to 1, under the map and ranges. Low values give foothills between ranges.
Slope of the beach face.

Mean beach width (m). It varies along the coast with noise, from none (cliffs) to twice this; the land behind blends down to it over 60 m. Land never lies at sea level: low coastal ground is lifted to at least 0.15 m plus [member beach_slope] over this width, then 2 m per km inland, and the erosion detail fades out over the first metres above the sea.
Metres between grid nodes. Coarse on purpose: this stage shapes ranges and valleys, finer detail is added on top.

With a recipe, [method generate] bakes its climate on the result (precipitation with the rain shadow, temperature by month and height, sunshine with horizons; the sea and lakes as water, cells of about its [member ClimateRecipe.sun_cell]) and feeds the rivers from a monthly water balance: [method get_runoff_at], [method get_snow_water_at], [method get_discharge_at] and the discharges of [method get_rivers] and [method get_waterfalls]. Snowmelt floods come in spring, summer evaporation lowers the rivers, lee slopes give less. Without one, every river carries [member river_runoff]. Costs about a tenth of the generation.

Coarse to fine, the V-cycle of Tzathas et al. (2024) with the time-stepping solver at every level: [member steps] run on a grid halved this many times (each halving a quarter of the cells), then each finer level starts from the bilinear upsample of the one below and runs [member refine_steps]. -1 halves while the coarse grid keeps at least 129 nodes a side (257: one level, 513: two, 1025: three); 0 runs every step at full resolution, as before. Needs [code](nodes - 1)[/code] even at each halving. About 2.1 times faster at 257 nodes, 3.1 at 513, 3.7 at 1025, with heights, slopes, crests and drainage density within 2% of the single-level result.
Distance (m) from each of [member ocean_edges] to the mean coastline.
How far (m) the coastline wanders either side of [member coast_distance], as bays and headlands.
Size (m) of the largest bays and headlands.
Steepest slope, in degrees, the rock holds along the flow direction; steeper ground collapses to it. 0 disables.
Optional [TerrainDeformer3D]. Its brushes are lifted before the write and applied again after it, and its terrain is used when [member terrain] is empty.

Sediment deposition, the [code]G[/code] of Yuan et al. 2019: [code]dh/dt = U - K A^m S + (G / A) Qs[/code], with [code]Qs[/code] the sediment carried from upstream. 0 keeps rivers cutting only. Where ranges rise out of ground that does not rise (low [member base_uplift]), about 0.5 makes the rivers leaving the mountains build flat alluvial plains with winding channels; higher values build fans up the range front. Where all the ground rises, deposition steepens the rivers instead and the mountains stand higher. Alluvium is added to [method get_sediment_depth]. Generation takes up to about 80% longer.
Slope the simulated ground is treated as having when steering the first gullies. Near the typical slope of the result.

Ridged noise on crests, as a share of twice the gully amplitude. Where opposite slopes meet (crests), the gullies fade to a share so they do not notch the crest into a regular comb, and this noise gives the crest irregular pinnacles and cols instead. 0 leaves crests to the gullies alone.
Gully depth as a fraction of its wavelength.

Carves gullies and spurs into the simulated ground with an erosion filter (Clay John 2018, Fewes 2023, Johansen 2026): stripes laid down the slope, octave by octave, each steered by the one before, faded towards peaks and valleys where the slope vanishes. Every point is computed on its own, so tiles join exactly and the result does not depend on threads.
Below 1, gullies are scaled down and the overall offset up by the inverse, which keeps peaks pointed.

Gully octaves, each half the wavelength of the one before. Keep the smallest ([member detail_wavelength] / 2^(octaves - 1)) at four terrain vertices or more, or it aliases into spikes; a configuration warning says when it does not.
How far smaller gullies reach from steep slopes onto gentler ground. Higher gives more detail.
Width of the largest gullies, in metres.
Stream power coefficient [code]K[/code]. Relief at equilibrium grows with [member uplift] / [member erodibility].

Falls of 4 m or more over hard rock (the strata's caprock) keep a vertical face: the ground holds the lip's height to the middle of the drop and the foot's after it, over 3 m, so the jet falls free. The grid alone holds a drop over a whole cell at best.

Drainage area is shared among all lower neighbours in proportion to slope to this power (multiple flow directions, Quinn et al. 1991, Freeman 1991). 0 routes all flow to the steepest neighbour (D8), which leaves straight 45 degree valleys.
The inspector's Generate button: runs [method bake].
A [MeshInstance3D] regenerated from a [HeightMapShape3D] ground after the write. The [member deformer]'s ground mesh is used when empty.
Added to every generated height.
Soil creep [code]k_d[/code] in square metres per year: rounds hilltops and softens ridges. 0 keeps sharp ridges.
Area (km²) an inflow marker without [code]area[/code] metadata brings in.

Markers ([Node3D]) where land beyond the map drains in: a river from upstream of the map edge, or a lake fed by a catchment behind its ridge. Metadata [code]area[/code] (km²), else [member inflow_area]. It enters at the marker's node (the nearest one off an outlet edge or the sea) and counts as that much drainage area in erosion, deposition, the rivers and their monthly discharge (at the rain and melt of the node it enters at). It brings no sediment. More metadata: [code]erosion[/code] (0..1, the share of that area that erodes; 0 brings water only), [code]sill[/code] (m: resistant rock round the entry, eroding 200 times slower and standing at 85 degrees) and [code]level[/code] (m: the sill is not worn below this height once uplift has raised it there). A marker with [code]sill[/code] or [code]level[/code] and no [code]area[/code] is a sill only.
Height of the seeded random roughness the simulation starts from, in metres.
Least drainage area (m²) above an automatic dam.

Number of automatic lakes. Valley cells with at least [member lake_catchment] draining through them, high enough above the sea and away from it, are tried in a seeded order; the largest lakes are built first, [member lake_spacing] apart.

Height (m) of a lake's dam above the valley floor: the deepest the lake can be at the dam. Lakes form behind natural dams (a moraine, landslide or rock bar) across a valley; the water stands at the dam's spillway, or at a lower col on the basin's rim, which then is the outlet.
Evaporation from a lake (mm/yr). A lake whose catchment's runoff ([member river_runoff]) is less than this over its area stands lower, where the two match, and has no outflow.
Smallest lake kept (m²).
Least distance (m) between automatic dams.

Lake markers (any [Node3D]): a dam at each, on the valley floor nearest to it, before the automatic ones. A [code]"depth"[/code] metadata overrides [member lake_depth]. By default the dam is a landslide dam whose downstream face slopes at 0.35 (19 degrees); on a steep reach that apron runs far down the valley and can bury a waterfall below the lake. A [code]"rock_lip"[/code] metadata set to [code]true[/code] makes the dam a bedrock sill with a face of about 72 degrees, so a lake can sit right above a fall and spill over it; [code]"face_slope"[/code] (rise over run) sets the face directly.
When above 0, the relief is scaled so the highest point is this far above [member sea_level]. 0 keeps the simulated heights.
Deepest the seabed goes (m below sea level).
Deepest soil and alluvium (basin fill comes on top).

Edges of the rectangle that are open sea (bits as in [member outlet_edges]). The sea cells are the run's outlets, held at sea level, so the land drains to the coast; set [member outlet_edges] to 0 to make the sea the only outlet.
Edges of the rectangle held at [member sea_level] where water leaves: bits [constant OUTLET_NEGATIVE_X], [constant OUTLET_POSITIVE_X], [constant OUTLET_NEGATIVE_Z], [constant OUTLET_POSITIVE_Z].
Publishes the geology map as the [code]terrain_geology_map[/code] and [code]terrain_geology_rect[/code] shader globals after each [method generate] (see [method get_geology_shader_code]).
Half width in metres of the uplift band around each Path3D in [member ranges]. A path's [code]width[/code] metadata overrides it, and its [code]uplift[/code] metadata sets its strength (default 1).
Path3D nodes along which mountain ranges rise.
Steps run at each finer level after [member coarse_levels] coarsened; enough for small valleys, hillslopes and sharp crests to form again at that resolution.

The month (0 January to 11 December) whose discharge [method get_rivers], [method get_waterfalls] and [method build_river_paths] use, -1 the annual mean: a spring flood or a late summer low. Needs a [member climate_recipe]; without one every month is the mean.
Mean runoff for river discharge without a [member climate_recipe], in mm a year (water reaching the channels per unit of drainage area).
River width per square root of discharge: [code]width = coefficient * discharge^0.5[/code] (hydraulic geometry, Leopold and Maddock 1953). About 7 for mean flows.
Height of the outlets and of the flat start.
Optional map over the rectangle: sea where it is white (red above 0.5), added to [member ocean_edges].
A in the equilibrium beach profile depth = A x^(2/3) at x metres offshore (Bruun 1954, Dean 1991); about 0.1 for fine sand, 0.2 for coarse.
Seed of the starting roughness. Different seeds give different drainage networks on the same uplift.
Slope added to the seabed past the surf zone (300 m offshore).
Width (X) and depth (Z) in metres of the rectangle generated, centred on the node.
Spacing in metres of the sky occlusion grid.
How far in metres each node looks for its horizon. Past the result the ground counts as level.
Seconds between reads of the sky for [member sky_light_source]. A read that finds the sky within 2% of the last one used changes nothing.

A [WorldEnvironment] or [Camera3D] whose sky lights the ground: its radiance is read back as a small panorama now and then ([member sky_light_interval]) and passed to [method update_sky_light]. Without it the seen sky is weighed as an even sky.

Bake the ground's horizons after [method generate], in 16 directions out to [member sky_distance], and from them the sky each node sees (see [method get_sky_image]). [TerrainMaterial3D] reads it for raster ambient light ([member TerrainMaterial3D.sky_occlusion_enabled]), so slopes the hills hide from part of the sky, such as a low sunset glow, do not take its light; the path tracer finds the hills itself.
Depth over which soil production halves, e-fold (h0 in Heimsath et al. 1997). Larger gives deeper soils.

Rate at which bare rock weathers into soil, in mm a year (P0 in Heimsath et al. 1997; measured 0.05 to 0.5). Ground eroding faster than this is bare rock: fast-rising ranges are bare, plains and gentle hills covered.
Time steps to simulate (on the coarsest grid when [member coarse_levels] coarsens).

Drainage area (m²) from which the bed stands as a cliff in hard rock and does not creep. Hard rock erodes slowly everywhere, but hillslopes in it still fail at [member critical_slope] (cliffs on every hillslope cell would leave pinnacles); 0 makes every cell a channel.
Steepest slope (degrees) hard rock stands at in a channel, and the soft rock right under a hard lip (worn back by the plunge pool, Scheingross and Lamb 2017).
Tilt of the layers (degrees). Near the slope of the rivers, a river runs along one band for long reaches and grades it into rapids instead of a fall.
The way the layers go down, degrees clockwise from north (-Z).

Layered rock: bands of hard rock in a sequence of soft rock, rising with the uplift (Forte, Yanites and Whipple 2016). Hard rock erodes [member strata_hardness] times slower; where a river has cut through a band into the soft rock under it, the undercut block breaks off and the face retreats upstream as a cliff (the caprock waterfall, Gilbert 1907; Haviv et al. 2010). Rivers step down over waterfalls ([method get_waterfalls]) between flatter reaches, and the range stands higher than in one rock. Off, the ground is the same as without these settings.
Share of each [member strata_spacing] that is hard rock: the thickness of the bands, and so the height of the falls.

How many times slower hard rock erodes than soft. Bedrock erosion goes as the inverse square of tensile strength (Sklar and Dietrich 2001), which spans more than ten times between mudstone and quartzite; below about 20, rivers grade the bands into steep rapids and few falls form.
Thickness (m) of one hard and one soft layer.
Metres the layer heights wander by (fbm noise of 700 m), so the bands do not follow contour lines exactly.
Angle of repose for scree: rock steeper than this sheds talus, which settles on slopes below it.
Distance below a cliff over which scree thins out.
The ground to write: a [code]Terrain3D[/code] node or a [CollisionShape3D] with a [HeightMapShape3D].
Extra ground eroded around each tile's core and cross-faded with its neighbours over its inner half, so droplets cut short at a tile's edge never show. About a quarter of the tile size.
Droplets per grid cell. More gives deeper, more connected rills.

Runs hydraulic and thermal erosion on a fine grid at the end of [method generate] (stage 4): droplet erosion (Beyer 2015, after Mei et al. 2007's capacity law) cutting rills and gullies and laying fans and valley fills, two layers (loose cover erodes first, bedrock at [member tile_erosion_rock_hardness]; Stava et al. 2008), and thermal slides of loose material steeper than [member talus_angle]. Overlapping tiles are eroded on their own, each seeded by its index, and cross-faded, so the result does not depend on threads. [method get_height] includes it; turning it off shows the ground without it.
Deepest cut and highest fill against the ground before tile erosion; erosion slows to nothing as a cut nears it, so channels cannot run away.
How fast bedrock erodes against loose cover (soil and scree from the geology maps, and settled sediment).
Grid spacing of the tile erosion. Around the terrain's vertex spacing; finer costs four times as much per halving.
Core size of each tile. Tiles are eroded in parallel.
Years per step. The solver is stable at any step; larger steps reach equilibrium sooner with less detail in the transient.
Uplift rate at full strength, in millimetres per year.
Uplift strength painted over the rectangle (red channel, 0 to 1).
Noise sampled at world X and Z that scales the uplift from the map and ranges down where it is low.
How far [member uplift_noise] can lower the uplift: where the noise is lowest the uplift is multiplied by [code]1 - strength[/code].

signal.description: Emitted when [method generate] or [method clear_result] starts, before any result is replaced. Work that reads the ground on other threads (a [Landscape3D] streaming its heights) finishes here.
